terms.grammar: cum with the indicative, or the subjunctive; tempus may be left out: fuit cum …
evidence: Cic. Inv. 1.2.2: fuit quoddam tempus cum in agrīs hominēs bēstiārum mōre vagābantur (Lewis & Short s.v. cum)
Varr. RR 3.1: fuit tempus cum rūra colerent hominēs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Latin says it as English does, with cum for “when”.

phrases.latin: fuit quoddam tempus cum in agrīs hominēs bēstiārum mōre vagābantur
phrases.english: there was a time when men wandered the fields like wild beasts

sources: Lewis & Short: cum · Lewis & Short: tempus
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 89, each phrase checked against the searchable text of the book.
Quotations marked “Lewis & Short” are given as Lewis & Short cites them, in the house spelling; they have not been checked against a modern edition.
